source_refs.note: Exercise 4.1, Question 4: book page 53 (PDF 58); answer key PDF 302

blocks.explanation:
Three results are asked: two products of \(A\) with its transpose, and the transpose of the transpose.
We must first write \(A^t\), then multiply in both orders (the answers have different orders), then transpose \(A^t\) again.
Plan: \(A^t\); orders; each entry of \(AA^t\) is (a row of \(A\))\(\cdot\)(a row of \(A\)), each entry of \(A^tA\) is (a column of \(A\))\(\cdot\)(a column of \(A\)).
steps:
Given: \(A\) of order \(3 \times 4\).
To find: \(AA^t\), \(A^tA\) and \((A^t)^t\).
Method: The transpose \(A^t\) is made by writing the rows of \(A\) as columns. Then row-by-column multiplication.

Write the transpose
\[A^t = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -3 \\ 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Row 1 of \(A\) becomes column 1 of \(A^t\), and so on. \(A\) is \(3 \times 4\), so \(A^t\) is \(4 \times 3\).

Find the order of each product
\[AA^t: (3 \times 4)(4 \times 3) \to 3 \times 3\]
\[A^tA: (4 \times 3)(3 \times 4) \to 4 \times 4\]
Why: The inner numbers match in both cases, so both products exist, but their orders are different, so \(AA^t \neq A^tA\).

Name the rows of \(A\)
\[R_1 = (-1, 2, 3, 0)\]
\[R_2 = (1, 0, 2, -2)\]
\[R_3 = (-3, 5, 3, -1)\]
Why: Column \(j\) of \(A^t\) is row \(j\) of \(A\), so entry \((i, j)\) of \(AA^t\) is \(R_i \cdot R_j\) (multiply matching entries and add).

Entries of \(AA^t\) on the diagonal
\[R_1 \cdot R_1 = 1 + 4 + 9 + 0 = 14\]
\[R_2 \cdot R_2 = 1 + 0 + 4 + 4 = 9\]
\[R_3 \cdot R_3 = 9 + 25 + 9 + 1 = 44\]
Why: A row times itself is the sum of the squares of its entries.

Entries of \(AA^t\) off the diagonal
\[R_1 \cdot R_2 = -1 + 0 + 6 + 0 = 5\]
\[R_1 \cdot R_3 = 3 + 10 + 9 + 0 = 22\]
\[R_2 \cdot R_3 = -3 + 0 + 6 + 2 = 5\]
Why: For example \(R_1 \cdot R_2 = (-1)(1) + (2)(0) + (3)(2) + (0)(-2)\). Since \(R_i \cdot R_j = R_j \cdot R_i\), entry \((2, 1)\) equals entry \((1, 2)\), and so on.

Write \(AA^t\)
\[AA^t = \begin{bmatrix}14 & 5 & 22 \\ 5 & 9 & 5 \\ 22 & 5 & 44\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Each value goes in its place \((i, j)\) and \((j, i)\). The matrix is symmetric.

Diagonal entries of \(A^tA\)
\[C_1 \cdot C_1 = 1 + 1 + 9 = 11\]
\[C_2 \cdot C_2 = 4 + 0 + 25 = 29\]
\[C_3 \cdot C_3 = 9 + 4 + 9 = 22\]
\[C_4 \cdot C_4 = 0 + 4 + 1 = 5\]
Why: Each is the sum of the squares of a column.

Other entries of \(A^tA\)
\[C_1 \cdot C_2 = -2 + 0 - 15 = -17\]
\[C_1 \cdot C_3 = -3 + 2 - 9 = -10\]
\[C_1 \cdot C_4 = 0 - 2 + 3 = 1\]
\[C_2 \cdot C_3 = 6 + 0 + 15 = 21\]
\[C_2 \cdot C_4 = 0 + 0 - 5 = -5\]
\[C_3 \cdot C_4 = 0 - 4 - 3 = -7\]
Why: For example \(C_1 \cdot C_2 = (-1)(2) + (1)(0) + (-3)(5)\). Each value is used in two symmetric places.

Transpose \(A^t\) again
\[(A^t)^t = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]
\[(A^t)^t = A\]
Why: Writing the rows of \(A^t\) as columns undoes the first transpose and gives \(A\) back.

Check
\[\text{tr}(AA^t) = 14 + 9 + 44 = 67\]
\[\text{tr}(A^tA) = 11 + 29 + 22 + 5 = 67\]
Why: Both diagonal sums equal the sum of the squares of all 12 entries of \(A\) (\(14 + 9 + 44 = 67\)), so the diagonals agree; and both products came out symmetric, as \(AA^t\) and \(A^tA\) always are.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The answer key prints
\[AA^t = \begin{bmatrix}14 & -5 & 8 \\ -5 & 9 & -11 \\ 8 & -11 & 44\end{bmatrix}\]
and
\[A^tA = \begin{bmatrix}11 & -3 & -6 & 1 \\ -3 & 29 & 19 & -5 \\ -6 & 19 & 22 & -4 \\ 1 & -5 & -4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]
These do not belong to the printed matrix \(A\). Only the diagonal entries are right. For example, entry (1, 2) of \(AA^t\) is \(R_1 \cdot R_2 = -1 + 0 + 6 + 0 = 5\), not \(-5\), and entry (1, 2) of \(A^tA\) is \(C_1 \cdot C_2 = -2 + 0 - 15 = -17\), not \(-3\). The correct products are the ones worked out above. The key's answer (iii) \((A^t)^t = A\) is correct.
